text: Automated containment isn't new in this path — SOAR playbooks that isolate a host, disable an account, or revoke a token the moment a detection fires were already covered as incident-response tooling. What this lesson adds is a design question: when should that automation actually fire first, and when should it wait for a human to approve it? That's not a question the SOAR platform answers for you. It's a decision an architecture review has to make, the same way blast radius got estimated in the last lesson.

Here's why automation can't just default to everywhere: an automated containment action has its own blast radius. Isolating a single compromised workstation that a detection flagged with high confidence is low blast radius — worst case, one employee loses access for an hour. But automatically isolating a production database, or disabling a shared service account that forty pipelines depend on, is high blast radius — a false positive there doesn't fail to help, it creates an outage that looks exactly like the incident it was supposed to stop.

The pattern that resolves this is tiered response, the same logic Lesson 15 used for admin credentials. Auto-contain with no approval needed, reserved for low-blast-radius, high-confidence actions: one workstation, one session, one IP. Auto-detect with a human-approved action for anything with real blast radius: a production server, a shared account, a trusted certificate. The platform still detects and prepares everything instantly either way — it just waits for a person to say yes before the high-impact step executes.

The dividing line is blast radius, not detection confidence, and that distinction matters. It's tempting to tier by how sure the detection is, but a high-confidence detection on a high-blast-radius resource still deserves a human in the loop, because the cost of being wrong is what should drive the decision — not just the odds of being right.

This closes the loop on the whole chapter. Assume breach said the architecture needs an answer ready before an incident. Blast radius gave the method for estimating what any one compromised thing — or any one automated response — could do. Lateral movement named the real paths attackers take and what interrupts each one. Automated isolation, built on exactly those estimates, is the fast last line that contains what got through, without becoming the next blast-radius problem itself.
